{{Short description|Mathematical notation based on the Arabic script}}
'''Modern Arabic mathematical notation''' is a [[mathematical notation]] based on the [[Arabic script]], used especially at [[pre-university]] levels of education. Its form is mostly derived from Western notation, but has some notable features that set it apart from its Western counterpart. The most remarkable of those features is the fact that it is written from right to left following the normal direction of the Arabic script. Other differences include the replacement of the [[Greek Alphabet|Greek]] and [[Latin alphabet]] letters for symbols with Arabic letters and the use of Arabic names for functions and relations.

==Features==
*It is written from right to left following the normal direction of the Arabic script. Other differences include the replacement of the [[Latin alphabet]] letters for symbols with Arabic letters and the use of Arabic names for functions and relations.
*The notation exhibits one of the very few remaining vestiges of [[rasm|non-dotted Arabic scripts]], as dots over and under letters (''[[i'jam]]'') are usually omitted.
*Letter cursivity (connectedness) of Arabic is also taken advantage of, in a few cases, to define variables using more than one letter. The most widespread example of this kind of usage is the canonical symbol for the radius of a circle '''{{lang|ar|؈}}''' ({{IPA|ar|nɑq}}), which is written using the two letters [[nun (letter)|nūn]] and [[qāf]]. When variable names are juxtaposed (as when expressing multiplication) they are written non-cursively.

==Variations==
Notation differs slightly from one region to another. In [[tertiary education]], most regions use the [[mathematical notation|Western notation]]. The notation mainly differs in numeral system used, and in mathematical symbols used.

=== Numeral systems ===
There are three numeral systems used in right to left mathematical notation.
*"[[Western Arabic numerals]]" (sometimes called European) are used in western Arabic regions (e.g. [[Morocco]])
*"[[Eastern Arabic numerals]]" are used in middle and eastern Arabic regions (e.g. [[Egypt]] and [[Syria]])
*"Eastern Arabic-Indic numerals" are used in [[Persian language|Persian]] and [[Urdu]] speaking regions (e.g. [[Iran]], [[Pakistan]], [[India]])

Written numerals are arranged with their lowest-value digit to the right, with higher value positions added to the left. That is identical to the arrangement used by Western texts using Hindu-Arabic numerals even though Arabic script is read from right to left: Indeed, Western texts are written with the ones digit on the right because when the arithmetical manuals were translated from the Arabic, the numerals were treated as figures (like in a Euclidean diagram), and so were not flipped to match the Left-Right order of Latin text.<ref>Oaks (2012). "[https://philarchive.org/archive/OAKASI-2 Algebraic symbolism in medieval Arabic algebra]" ''Philosophia, 87'' 27--83.</ref> The symbols "٫" and  "٬"  may be used as the [[decimal mark]] and the [[Decimal mark#Digit grouping|thousands separator]] respectively when writing with Eastern Arabic numerals, e.g. {{lang|ar| ٣٫١٤١٥٩٢٦٥٣٥٨ }} ''3.14159265358'', {{lang|ar| ١٬٠٠٠٬٠٠٠٬٠٠٠ }} ''1,000,000,000''. Negative signs are written to the left of magnitudes, e.g. {{lang|ar| ٣− }} ''−3''. In-line fractions are written with the numerator and denominator on the left and right of the fraction slash respectively, e.g. {{lang|ar| ٢/٧ }} ''2/7''.{{citation needed|date=August 2024}}

===Symbols===

Sometimes, symbols used in Arabic mathematical notation differ according to the region:

{| class="wikitable"
| colspan=3 |[[Image:Difference between arabic and persian maths limit.PNG|500px|Arabic mathematical limit in different forms]]
|-
! style="width: 150px;" | Latin
! style="width: 150px;" | Arabic
! style="width: 150px;" | Persian
|-
| {{math| {{underset| ''x''→∞ | lim }} ''x''<sup>4</sup> }}
| {{math| {{lang|rtl=yes|ar-Zmth|س<sup>٤</sup> {{underset| س←∞&rlm; |نهــــــــــــا}} }} }}{{ref|a|[a]}}
| {{math| {{lang|rtl=yes|fa-Zmth|س<sup>۴</sup> {{underset| س←∞&rlm; | حــــــــــــد }} }} }}{{ref|b|[b]}}
|}
{{refbegin}}
* {{note|a|a}} {{lang|ar-Zmth|نهــــا}} ''nūn''-''hāʾ''-''ʾalif'' is derived from the first three letters of [[Arabic language|Arabic]] {{lang|ar|نهاية}}  ''nihāya'' "limit".
* {{note|b|b}} {{lang|fa|حد}} ''ḥadd'' is [[Persian language|Persian]] for "limit".
{{refend}}

Sometimes, mirrored Latin and Greek symbols are used in Arabic mathematical notation (especially in western Arabic regions):

{| class="wikitable"
| colspan=3 |[[Image:Difference between arabic mathematical sum forms.PNG|500px|Arabic mathematical sum in different forms]]
|-
! style="width: 150px;" | Latin
! style="width: 150px;" | Arabic
! style="width: 150px;" | Mirrored Latin and Greek
|-
| {{math| {{underoverset| ∑ | ''n'' | ''x''{{=}}0 }} {{radic|''x''|3}} }}
| {{math|1={{lang|rtl=yes|ar-Zmth|2=<sup style="margin-left: -0.5em; vertical-align: 0.8em;">٣</sup><span style="{{mirrorH}}">&#x202d;√&#x202c;</span>{{overline|س}} {{underoverset| مجــــــــــــ | ں | س{{=}}٠ }} }}}}{{ref|c|[c]}}
| {{math|1={{lang|rtl=yes|ar-Zmth|2=&#x202a;<span style="{{mirrorH}}">√</span><sup style="margin-left: -0.5em; vertical-align: 0.8em;">3</sup>&#x202c;{{overline|س}} {{underoverset|1=<span style="{{mirrorH}}">&#x202d;∑&#x202c;</span> |2=ں |3= س{{=}}0 }} }}}}
|}
{{refbegin}}
* {{note|c|c}} {{lang|ar|مجــــ}} is derived from [[Arabic language|Arabic]] {{lang|ar|مجموع}} ''maǧmūʿ'' "sum".
{{refend}}

However, in Iran, usually Latin and Greek symbols are used.

However, according to others there is no historical evidence for this.<ref>{{cite book|last=Cajori|first=Florian|title=A History of Mathematical Notation|year=1993|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofmathema00cajo_0|url-access=registration|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|accessdate=11 October 2012|pages=[https://archive.org/details/historyofmathema00cajo_0/page/382 382]–383|isbn=9780486677668|quote=Nor is there historical evidence to support the statement found in Noah Webster's Dictionary, under the letter x, to the effect that 'x was used as an abbreviation of Ar. shei (a thing), something, which, in the Middle Ages, was used to designate the unknown, and was then prevailingly transcribed as xei.'}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Oxford Dictionary, 2nd Edition|quote=There is no evidence in support of the hypothesis that x is derived ultimately from the mediaeval transliteration xei of shei "thing", used by the Arabs to denote the unknown quantity, or from the compendium for L. res "thing" or radix "root" (resembling a loosely-written x), used by mediaeval mathematicians.}}</ref>

| From {{lang|ar| جذ }} ''jīm''-''ḏāl''. The Arabic word for "product" is جداء ''jadāʾun''. Also <math>\prod</math> in some regions.
|-
| [[Factorial]]
| <math>n!</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical factorial.PNG|30px]]
| {{math| {{lang|ar|2=<span style="border-bottom: 1px #000 solid; border-right: 1px #000 solid; display: inline; line-height: 1em; padding: 0 0.25em;">ں</span>}} }}
| Also [[Image:Arabic mathematical fact.PNG|30px]] ({{math| {{lang|ar|ں!}} }}) in some regions
|-
| [[Permutations]]
| <math>^n\mathbf{P}_r</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical nPr.PNG|50px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar|<sup>ں</sup>ل<sub>ر</sub>}} }}
| Also [[Image:Arabic mathematical P(n,r).PNG|75px]] ({{math| {{lang|ar| ل(ں، ر) }} }}) is used in some regions as <math>\mathbf{P}(n,r)</math>
|-
| [[Combinations]]
| <math>^n\mathbf{C}_k</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical nCk.PNG|50px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar|<sup>ں</sup>ٯ<sub>ك</sub>}} }}
| Also [[Image:Arabic mathematical C(n,k).PNG|75px]] ({{math| {{lang|ar| ٯ(ں، ك) }} }}) is used in some regions as <math>\mathbf{C}(n,k) </math> and [[Image:Arabic mathematical b(n,k).PNG|40px]]  ({{math|{{ldelim|a=round|b=1}}{{su|lh=1.8|va=middle|p=ں|b=ك}}{{rdelim|a=round|b=1}}}} ) as the [[binomial coefficient]] <math> n \choose k</math>
|-
|}

| Sine
| <math>\sin</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical sin.PNG|20px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| حا }} }}
| from {{lang|ar|حاء}} ''ḥāʾ'' (i.e. dotless {{lang|ar|ج}} ''jīm'')-''ʾalif''; also [[Image:Arabic mathematical sins.PNG|30px]] ({{math|{{lang|ar|جب}}}} ''jīm''-''bāʾ'') is used in some regions (e.g. Syria); Arabic for "sine" is {{lang|ar| جيب }} ''jayb''
|-
| Cosine
| <math>\cos</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical cos.PNG|25px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| حتا }} }}
| from {{lang|ar| حتا }} ''ḥāʾ'' (i.e. dotless {{lang|ar| ج }} ''jīm'')-''tāʾ''-''ʾalif''; also [[Image:Arabic mathematical coss.PNG|30px]] ({{math|{{lang|ar|تجب}}}} ''tāʾ''-''jīm''-''bāʾ'') is used in some regions (e.g. Syria); Arabic for "cosine" is {{lang|ar| جيب تمام }}
|-
| Tangent
| <math>\tan</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical tan.PNG|25px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| طا }} }}
| from {{lang|ar| طا }} ''ṭāʾ'' (i.e. dotless {{lang|ar| ظ }} ''ẓāʾ'')-''ʾalif''; also [[Image:Arabic mathematical tans.PNG|30px]] ({{math|{{lang|ar|ظل}}}} ''ẓāʾ''-''lām'') is used in some regions (e.g. Syria); Arabic for "tangent" is {{lang|ar| ظل }} ''ẓill''
|-
| Cotangent
| <math>\cot</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical cot.PNG|25px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| طتا }} }}
| from {{lang|ar| طتا }} ''ṭāʾ'' (i.e. dotless {{lang|ar| ظ }} ''ẓāʾ'')-''tāʾ''-''ʾalif''; also [[Image:Arabic mathematical cots.PNG|30px]] ({{math|{{lang|ar|تظل}}}} ''tāʾ''-''ẓāʾ''-''lām'') is used in some regions (e.g. Syria); Arabic for "cotangent" is {{lang|ar| ظل تمام }}
|-
| Secant
| <math>\sec</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical sec.PNG|18px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯا }} }}
| from {{lang|ar| ٯا }} dotless {{lang|ar| ق }} ''qāf''-''ʾalif''; Arabic for "secant" is {{lang|ar| قاطع }}
|-
| Cosecant
| <math>\csc</math>
| [[Image:Arabic mathematical csc.PNG|25px]] || {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯتا }} }}

====[[Hyperbolic functions]]====
The letter [[Image:Arabic mathematical zain.PNG|20px]] ({{math|{{lang|ar|ز}}}} ''zayn'', from the first letter of the second word of {{lang|ar|دالة زائدية}} "hyperbolic function") is added to the end of trigonometric functions to express hyperbolic functions. This is similar to the way <math>\operatorname{h}</math> is added to the end of trigonometric functions in Latin-based notation.
{| class="wikitable"
| colspan=7 | [[Image:Arabic mathematical hf.PNG|500px|Arabic hyperbolic functions]]
|-
! style="font-size:80%; width:70px;" | Description
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic sine
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic cosine
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic tangent
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic cotangent
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic secant
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Hyperbolic cosecant
|-
! style="font-size:80%; width:70px;" | Latin
| <math>\sinh</math> || <math>\cosh</math> || <math>\tanh</math> || <math>\coth</math> || <math>\operatorname{sech}</math> || <math>\operatorname{csch}</math>
|-
! style="font-size:80%; width:70px;" | Arabic
| {{math| {{lang|ar| حاز }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| حتاز }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| طاز }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| طتاز }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯاز }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯتاز }} }}
|}

====[[Inverse trigonometric functions]]====
For inverse trigonometric functions, the superscript {{math| {{lang|ar| −١ }} }} in Arabic notation is similar in usage to the superscript <math>-1</math> in Latin-based notation.

| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Inverse tangent
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Inverse cotangent
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Inverse secant
| style="font-size:80%; width:60px;" | Inverse cosecant
|-
! style="font-size:80%; width:70px;" | Latin

|-
! style="font-size:80%; width:70px;" | Arabic
| {{math| {{lang|ar| حا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| حتا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| طا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| طتا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
| {{math| {{lang|ar| ٯتا<sup>−١</sup> }} }}
|}
